paper.title_en: Modified gravity bridges the cosmological tensions
paper.abstract_en: The standard model of cosmology, <math display="inline"><mi mathvariant="normal">Λ</mi></math> cold dark matter (<math display="inline"><mi mathvariant="normal">Λ</mi><mi>CDM</mi></math>), is plagued by various tensions with recent observations. The most pressing one is the Hubble tension, where the observed expansion rate of our Universe is <math display="inline"><mn>5</mn><mi>σ</mi></math> larger than that predicted by <math display="inline"><mi mathvariant="normal">Λ</mi><mi>CDM</mi></math>. Recently, the result from DESI also reveals a new inconsistency between the baryon acoustic oscillation and cosmic microwave background (CMB) observations in <math display="inline"><mi mathvariant="normal">Λ</mi><mi>CDM</mi></math>. It is found that these major cosmological tensions can be traced back to a common physical origin—the nonminimal coupling between gravity and matter, different from the expectation of general relativity (GR). Bayesian model comparison reveals strong evidence of nonminimally coupled gravity over GR and <math display="inline"><mi mathvariant="normal">Λ</mi><mi>CDM</mi></math>, with a Bayes factor <math display="inline"><mi>ln</mi><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>12.1</mn></math>. The nonminimal coupling model predicts that gravity in the early Universe should be <math display="inline"><mo>∼</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>%</mo></math> stronger on cosmological scales than it is today, which is consistent with current observation and will be tested by upcoming CMB and big bang nucleosynthesis experiments.
